title: Young Indian Wrestlers Denied US Visas Ahead of U23 World Championships in Las Vegas
excerpt: The Wrestling Federation of India has urged the US Embassy in New Delhi to reconsider the rejected cases and grant visas to wrestlers appearing for appointments on Thursday, ahead of the October 12–18 tournament.
body:
• Several young Indian wrestlers have been denied US visas ahead of the U23 World Wrestling Championships in Las Vegas (October 12–18), jeopardizing India's participation in the tournament.
  • The Wrestling Federation of India has urged the US Embassy in New Delhi to reconsider the cases, and has asked the embassy to grant visas to the wrestlers scheduled to appear for their consular appointments on Thursday.
  • The rejections reportedly turned on the athletes' profiles — under-20 and unemployed — the classic grounds on which consular officers deny visas over doubts the applicant will return home.
  • This is not the first time visa trouble has hit an Indian wrestling squad: in 2022, Spain denied visas to 21 Indian wrestlers for the U23 Worlds in Pontevedra on similar overstay suspicions.

Indian wrestling's next generation has run into a wall before even reaching the mat. Several young Indian wrestlers have been denied US visas ahead of the U23 World Wrestling Championships in Las Vegas, prompting the Wrestling Federation of India to seek an urgent review of the decisions.

The WFI has urged the US Embassy in New Delhi to reconsider the rejected cases, and has specifically requested the embassy to grant visas to the wrestlers who are scheduled to appear for their consular appointments on Thursday, according to reporting on the development.

Why the visas were refused

The denials appear to turn on the athletes' profiles rather than their credentials: under-20 and unemployed. That combination is the classic trigger for refusals under US immigration law's immigrant-intent presumption, which requires every visa applicant to convince the consular officer they will return home after their visit. For teenage athletes with no job, property or travel history to point to, clearing that bar can be difficult — even when they carry government clearances and an invitation from the sport's world governing body.

The timing could hardly be worse. The 2026 U23 World Championships run October 12–18 at the Thomas & Mack Center in Las Vegas — the first time the United States has hosted the U23 Worlds, and the first World Championships of any age group on American soil since 2015. More than 600 wrestlers are expected, and United World Wrestling's entry lists already include Indian competitors across the men's freestyle weight classes.

A familiar nightmare for Indian wrestling

Indian wrestling has lived through this exact scenario before. In October 2022, the Spanish Embassy denied visas to 21 members of India's 30-strong squad for the U23 World Championships in Pontevedra, on suspicion the wrestlers might overstay — despite the WFI presenting government clearance and an invitation from United World Wrestling. Only nine wrestlers made that trip, and it was the first time in the competition's history that India failed to field a full team.

Then, as now, the federation called the decision bizarre and high-handed, and took the matter to the world body. The recurrence four years later — this time at a tournament the United States itself is hosting — underscores how little protection sporting credentials offer against consular discretion.

Diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora in the US, which turns out in force for wrestling events, the irony is sharp: a home-soil world championship that Indian fans in Las Vegas may watch without India's full squad. More broadly, the episode lands in a year when US visa scrutiny has tightened across categories — from student programs to work authorizations — and young Indians are feeling it first.

What's next

Everything now hinges on the embassy's response to the WFI's plea — and on Thursday's appointments for the wrestlers still in the queue. If reconsideration fails, India could head to Las Vegas shorthanded for the second U23 Worlds in a row, and the federation will again be left asking the world body why host nations keep shutting its athletes out.
